      How strong is a PIN?

      Each digit adds log₂ 10 ≈ 3.3 bits, so even an 8-digit PIN has fewer combinations than a 6-character password. That is fine, because a PIN is not meant to survive an offline attack: it guards a card or device that locks, wipes or gets blocked after a few wrong tries.

      The last column is the brute-force time with no lockout at all, for comparison with passwords. With a card blocked after three wrong attempts, a random 4-digit PIN gives a thief a 3 in 10,000 chance.

      PINs to avoid

      An analysis of 3.4 million leaked four-digit PINs by DataGenetics found that 1234 alone accounted for about one in ten, and the twenty most common PINs for over a quarter. Attackers try these first:

      • Sequences and repeats: 1234, 0000, 1111, 1212, 7777, 4321 and 2580 (straight down the keypad).
      • Dates: years such as 1985 or 2010, and birthdays written as DDMM or MMDD — easy to find on social media.
      • Your other numbers: the end of your phone number, your house number or an old PIN.

      Using a generated PIN

      • Banks usually let you change a card PIN at a cash machine or in their app — generate it here, set it there.
      • Choose 6 digits for a phone and anywhere else that allows it.
      • Never write it on the card or keep it next to it; a password manager's secure notes are a better place.

      Questions people ask

      Is a 4-digit PIN secure enough?

      For a bank card that is blocked after three wrong attempts, yes — as long as it is random. For a phone, prefer 6 digits or a passphrase: a phone is a bigger prize and some allow more attempts.

      Why does a random PIN sometimes look like a pattern?

      Truly random PINs include every combination equally often, 1212 and 0007 included. Filtering out “ugly” PINs would make the rest more predictable. If one looks too memorable for comfort, generate another.

      Can I generate many PINs at once?

      Yes. Set “How many at once” up to 50, then copy them all or download them as a text file — handy for door codes, test data or one-time codes.

      Is anything sent to a server?

      No. Everything is generated in your browser tab with the Web Crypto API, and the page's Content Security Policy blocks every network request — open your browser's network panel and watch it stay empty. Only your settings are remembered on your device; generated values never are.
